body.text:
Fixed — the docs commit is now clean (5 files: the two plan docs, README, CLI_PLAN pointer, and the handoff move), and the M10 agent's in-progress work sits untouched in the working tree (it has since wired `bin.ts` and written its test file, so it's in its verification phase).

Summary of what changed for your two asks:

**Plans now reflect the smaller service surface.** [MONOREPO_PLAN.md](architecture/MONOREPO_PLAN.md) §5.1 carries a **VALIDATED 2026-07-18** banner recording the real-GitHub round-trip, and §5.3's ref-relay tier is marked **NOT BEING BUILT** — kept only as a record of what was considered and why it's unnecessary. The server package's entire scope is now the shared-index/query tier (Fastify + pgvector), gated on a second machine/person actually existing. [PLAN_2026-07-18.md](architecture/PLAN_2026-07-18.md)'s surface table and W1 item 5 say the same thing: M13 `sync` targets any ordinary git remote, and the hosting story for sync is a paragraph of documentation.

**Root is tidied.** `HANDOFF.md` is archived as [architecture/HANDOFF_2026-07-17.md](architecture/HANDOFF_2026-07-17.md), and the README's resume pointer now leads with the current plan doc plus `git for-ai log --intent` as ground truth. The repo root is down to `README.md` and real project files. (The `ideas/` and `research/` directories are still top-level — they're original design material rather than session planning; say the word if you'd like those folded under `architecture/` or a `docs/` tree too.)

One process note in the spirit of honest reporting: my docs commit initially swept in the agent's half-written `reindex.ts` via a careless `git add -u`; I caught it on the immediate post-commit check and redid the commit without it, same message and Change-Id, so identity tracking carried over cleanly. Explicit-path staging only from here on while agents share the tree.

M10 should report shortly; then it's verify → commit → M11.

Slightly ahead of the approved ordering, but less than you might think — and there's a version of "start the UI now" that's actually sound.

The approved order was: finish the CLI (M10–M12, then sync/doctor) → MCP server → review UI. The reason `ask`/`blame --why` came first was the assumption that a UI needs the query engine. But breaking the review UI into its parts changes the picture:

**Buildable today, no M11/M12 needed:** the timeline (commits × agents × changes), the change-detail view (diff beside reasoning, confidence/risk flags), and the session-trace narrative all read data that already exists — ledger, sessions, change-map, all reachable through `core` right now. Same for the `report` digest command, which the plan already flagged as "can come earlier."

**Genuinely blocked on M11/M12:** only the semantic parts — an "ask" box and any "why is this line like this" navigation. That's one panel of the UI, not its skeleton.

So the honest framing: you're not ahead on the *review* surface; you'd only be ahead if you wanted the *query* surface in a UI before the query engine exists.

My recommendation: let M10 land (the agent is in its verification phase now), start the M11 agent on the query engine, and — since they touch entirely different code — begin the review surface in parallel, `report` first. `report` is a day-scale item that forces every "what does a human actually want to see" decision cheaply, and the SPA then renders what `report` proved out, with the ask panel slotting in when M12 lands. That gets you the "prove it to me" surface you named as core to the vision weeks earlier than the strict sequence would, at no real cost — the one discipline required is separate agents in separate packages, which is the pattern we've been running all day anyway.

If you'd rather keep strict order (query engine before any UI work), that's also defensible — it just delays the thing you said matters most. Your call: parallel-start `report` + UI, or strict sequence?

Completely fair — and that's the strongest possible argument for pulling the visible surface forward. Let's get you something you can actually look at. Launching an agent right now to build `git for-ai report`: a self-contained HTML digest of everything your agents have done in this repo — timeline, per-change intent, reasoning flags, session evidence — openable in your browser today:

That impatience is legitimate, and it's now driving the roadmap: a **report agent is building `git for-ai report`** as we speak — when it lands (likely within the half hour) there'll be a `report.html` you double-click and browse: the full timeline of what your agents did in this repo, each change's intent and rejected alternatives, confidence and risk flags, and the session evidence underneath. That file is the seed of the review UI — same information design, static first.

Meanwhile, two things you can do *right now* in your own terminal that are more tangible than anything I've been relaying secondhand:

```
git for-ai log --intent
```
— your repo's history annotated with what each change was *for*, who made it (agent + model, or you), and confidence. Notice `cab14f1` says `[human]` — that's your plan approval, recorded by you via `annotate` this morning.

```
git for-ai show 8e25afb --session
```
— the M7 commit with its full captured session: 348 spans of the actual working session that built it, redacted, permanently attached, and (since this morning's push) backed up on GitHub.

And one reframe worth holding onto: the reason today *felt* invisible is that most of it was the plumbing that makes the visible stuff trustworthy — identity that survives rewrites, capture that can't break a commit, an index layer, sync with no server. The visible layer (report → review SPA → `ask`) is exactly what's being built next, and it's thin *because* the plumbing underneath it is done. Two agents are running now — M10's reindex in verification, the report builder just started — and I'll wire both in and hand you the HTML the moment it exists.

The M10 agent had paused with its real-model dogfood run still in flight — I've resumed it with instructions to finish the run, do the second incremental pass (the proof that unchanged content re-embeds nothing), and deliver its full report. Both agents are now working in the background: M10 finishing verification, and the report builder creating your first browsable HTML digest. I'll verify and wire everything in as each one lands.

Still in a holding pattern on M10 — the agent's real-model reindex run is grinding through the first full index of this repo (model inference over every chunk of code, ledger, and session content; the slow part is one-time). It has progress checks armed and will resume itself as the run advances. The report builder is also still working. Nothing needs your input — I'll verify and commit each as it completes, and your `report.html` gets handed over the moment it exists.

attributes.command:
cd C:/src/git-for-ai/packages/cli && pnpm vitest run src/commands/report.test.ts 2>&1 | tail -3 && cd ../.. && git add packages/cli/src/commands/report.ts packages/cli/src/commands/report.test.ts && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
Add `report` command logic: the first human-visible surface

runReport() generates a self-contained HTML (or Markdown) digest of
agent activity per PLAN_2026-07-18.md §2.2: stat header, newest-first
timeline with author/provenance/confidence/risk badges, and per-change
detail cards pairing every claim with its evidence (tested, scope,
session capture line). Zero JS (native <details>), no external
requests, dark/light aware, three explicit degradation labels — honest
data only. Non-minting reads verified: report runs leave the
change-map byte-identical.

Built by a background Fable 5 agent; 10 real-fixture tests passing,
independently re-run before commit. bin.ts wiring lands with M10's
(the other in-flight agent owns that file).

Generated live on this repo: .git-for-ai/report.html — 17 commits, 12
changes, 9 sessions, 2 models.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)"

summary: claude-code session: 5 tool execution(s), 6 model turn(s) for commit "Add `report` command logic: the first human-visible surface".
